known_from_text.basis: Verses 3–5 name the night-long hand gesture, the soul's refusal, the fainting spirit, eyelids held open, and inability to speak.
known_from_text.claim: The speaker's distress includes sleeplessness, agitation, failed speech, and refusal of comfort.

known_from_text.basis: Verse 2 says 'he listens to me'; verses 3–10 continue the lament without reporting rescue.
known_from_text.claim: The setting juxtaposes God's listening with continuing distress.

known_from_text.basis: Verses 8–10 repeatedly ask 'Will' and 'Has,' retaining the interrogative form.
known_from_text.claim: The feared end of God's favor is expressed as questioning, not as an established conclusion.

known_from_text.basis: Remembering God accompanies groaning in verse 4; verses 12–13 make remembrance and reflection deliberate commitments that lead into praise.
known_from_text.claim: Remembrance changes function during the poem.

known_from_text.basis: Verse 11 explicitly reads 'those years of the right hand'; the supplied verse-level evidence also records a competing changing interpretation.
known_from_text.claim: The English selects the years interpretation of the difficult hinge verse.

known_from_text.basis: Verse 16 identifies Jacob's and Joseph's children; verse 20 places God's way through the sea; verse 21 names Moses and Aaron.
known_from_text.claim: The closing remembrance evokes Israel's sea deliverance and guidance under Moses and Aaron.

known_from_text.basis: Waters see and writhe in verse 17, skies raise their voice in verse 18, and thunder has a voice in verse 19. Arrows, footprints, arm, hand, and flock remain visible.
known_from_text.claim: The natural world is personified rather than explained away.

not_known_from_text.claim: The historical identity of the first-person speaker or the individual composer.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The heading's Asaph association does not identify the speaking 'I' or independently establish personal authorship.

not_known_from_text.claim: The date and specific crisis that prompted the lament.
not_known_from_text.why_not: Distress is described without naming an event, enemy, ruler, illness, or location.

not_known_from_text.claim: That the speaker's present distress has been resolved.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The ending recalls communal guidance; it does not report a present answer, recovery, or renewed comfort.

not_known_from_text.claim: A specific festival, sanctuary ceremony, or division among soloists and choir.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The musical heading and markers provide no detailed ritual or vocal assignment.

not_known_from_text.claim: The exact original performance meaning of Selah or the ancient meter and instrumentation.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The markers are present, but the supplied text contains no instructions defining their execution or a musical score.

not_known_from_text.claim: That the poem supplies a literal meteorological record or identifies a particular sea-crossing location.
not_known_from_text.why_not: The storm and sea are presented poetically, and no geographical site is named.

guardrails.cultic_setting: The director heading and Selah markers support a musical or liturgical horizon. The first-person night distress supplies a voiced situation within that horizon, while the ancestral names, redeemed people, sea passage, and Moses and Aaron ground the remembrance in Israel's communal deliverance tradition. The text does not identify a particular service, festival, temple location, or ritual. This English chooses 'your way is holy' in verse 14, so it does not explicitly locate that verse in a sanctuary.
guardrails.heading_attribution: The heading designates a psalm, addresses a director interpreted as musical, and associates the composition with Jeduthun and Asaph. 'Of Asaph' conveys the traditional ascription; it does not independently establish that a particular historical Asaph personally composed these words. 'For Jeduthun' leaves the precise relationship broad and does not establish whether Jeduthun is a recipient, performer, or reference to a performance tradition. No date or historical occasion is named.

analyses.method: Compared the whole English setting with the supplied Hebrew forms, token evidence, and literal backbones, attending to speaker, agency, imagery, verbal movement, and retained Selah markers. Token forms took precedence over displaced lexical metadata; tokens supply material missing from the displayed Hebrew lines in verses 1, 12, and 20. Section titles are analytical divisions, not supplied arrangement labels. Translation resemblance was assessed against the three supplied English texts and identified recollections, without treating resemblance as proof of dependence. No external editions or lexica were consulted.

non_source_material.note: Earlier translator guidance for this setting, not Hebrew content or an added line in the lyric. No score is supplied to verify its musical realization.

sections.arc_note: Frames the lyric for performance and associates it with Jeduthun and Asaph without supplying an occasion.
sections.title: Heading

sections.arc_note: The assertion that God listens gives way to the extended hand, groaning, and a fainting spirit. Remembering God initially intensifies distress. Selah closes the movement.
sections.theme: Calling to God while comfort remains refused.
sections.title: Cry and Unrelieved Distress

sections.arc_note: Direct accusation—God holds the eyelids open—turns toward former days and a remembered night song. The searching spirit prepares the questions that follow.
sections.title: Sleepless Recollection

sections.arc_note: Parallel questions intensify from rejection to the possibility that God has forgotten kindness or closed away compassion. They receive no immediate verbal answer; Selah remains at their end.
sections.theme: Whether rejection, lost favor, and withheld compassion are permanent.
sections.title: Questions About Abandonment

sections.arc_note: The strained statement about the Most High's right-hand years bridges doubt and remembrance. Repeated 'I'll' declarations establish a chosen activity, without asserting that the distress has ended.
sections.theme: Affliction and the resolve to recount God's deeds.
sections.title: Grief Turning Toward Remembrance

sections.arc_note: Reflection becomes direct praise, moving from God's holy way to publicly known strength and the arm that freed Jacob's and Joseph's children. Selah marks the close.
sections.theme: God's incomparable greatness and deliverance of his people.
sections.title: Holiness, Wonder, and Redemption

sections.arc_note: Repeated seeing becomes writhing and trembling; clouds, voices, arrows, thunder, and lightning enlarge the remembered scene until the earth itself shakes.
sections.theme: Creation's bodily response to God's presence.
sections.title: Waters and Storm

sections.arc_note: The holy 'way' returns as a route through the sea. Unknown footprints preserve mystery, while the flock and the hand of Moses and Aaron provide a quieter conclusion.
sections.theme: A passage through water and guidance mediated through human leaders.
sections.title: Untraceable Way and Guided Flock

similar_translations.evidence: The strongest supplied cluster occurs at MT verses 4–5: remembering God with groaning and 'You hold my eyelids open.' MT verse 17 shares the waters' writhing, and verses 19–20 share the whirlwind and paths through great waters. Differences include this setting's holy-way reading at verse 14, grief at verse 11, and explicit arrows flying back and forth.

Recalled similarities cluster at MT verses 4–5 in groaning, a fainting spirit, and eyelids held open; at verse 14 in 'your way is holy'; and at verse 17 in writhing waters and trembling depths. These are local echoes, not evidence that the setting reproduces that translation.

MT verse 3 retains the hand and lack of slackening, unlike the supplied KJV's sore. Verse 12's recounting of deeds resembles the ASV's mention-of-deeds choice. Verses 19–20 share the whirlwind interpretation and plural paths. At verse 11 both retain years, but this setting omits the ASV's supplied recollection clause.

Limited echoes appear in the combination at MT verse 11 of personal affliction with right-hand years, and at verse 10 in compassion being shut up rather than merely withheld. These choices are also shared with the ASV. The setting diverges from distinctive KJV readings at verses 3, 14, and 19: sore, sanctuary, and heaven.

analyses.summary: The setting moves from a repeated cry through sleeplessness and increasingly severe questions about God's faithfulness into deliberate remembrance of deliverance. Short lines and contractions keep the lament conversational; repeated voice, remembrance, way, and bodily imagery connect its movements. Verse 11 retains the difficult 'years of the right hand' reading without turning it into confident reassurance. The remembered storm expands the scene from one troubled person to waters, skies, and earth, before the ending settles on untraceable footprints and a flock guided through Moses and Aaron. Remembered guidance closes the poem, but the speaker never explicitly reports relief from the present distress. All three instances of Selah remain.
